fixes.explanation: True. Mark 3:21 says His family went out to take custody of Him, saying, "He is out of His mind." That's a hard thing to hear about Jesus from the people closest to Him. I think this one stings a little.

It's the other way around. Mark 3:21 says His family went out to take custody of Him, saying, "He is out of His mind." So the words really were said. I think it's a heavy line, and the passage doesn't hide it.
Paying off servants is a whole heist movie, baker. Jesus doesn't go there. He says the thief has to first tie up the strong man (Mark 3:27). No servants and no payments in that picture.

He has an unclean spirit, yes. Mark 3:30 says Jesus made this statement because they were saying, "He has an unclean spirit." The writer gives us the reason outright, so we don't have to guess. Good reading, baker.

The Sabbath did come up with Jesus earlier in Mark (Mark 3:1–6), so I see why that popped up. But here, Mark gives a different reason. Jesus made this statement because they were saying, "He has an unclean spirit." (Mark 3:30). That's the charge in this scene.

Speaking against Moses is a serious charge, but it's not in this passage. Mark 3:30 says Jesus made this statement because they were saying, "He has an unclean spirit." That's the one the writer names.
Leave makes sense if you picture a packed house. But the text never says they were stuck inside. It says they "…could not even eat." So the problem was getting to eat, friend.

The Pharisees are a big name, so I get the pick. They aren't in this part of the story, though. The people who came down from Jerusalem here are scribes (Mark 3:22), and they're doing something different. The ones taking custody are His family (Mark 3:21).
Elijah is a big name, so I see where you were going. But the scribes didn't name him at all. They said, "By the prince of the demons He drives out demons." (Mark 3:22). Elijah isn't in this story.

The Holy Spirit is right. Jesus says, "But whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will never be forgiven; he is guilty of eternal sin." (Mark 3:29). That's a serious line. Mark tells us in verse 30 what was being said when Jesus spoke it.

The prophets are a natural guess, but Jesus doesn't name them here. He says it's "…whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit…" who "…will never be forgiven…" (Mark 3:29). That's a heavy verse, so it's worth getting the name right.

True. Jesus says whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit "…will never be forgiven; he is guilty of eternal sin." (Mark 3:29). It follows His line that the sons of men will be forgiven all sins and blasphemies (Mark 3:28). Mark ties it to what was being said in verse 30 (Mark 3:30).

Jesus really does say it. Mark 3:29 reads, "But whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will never be forgiven; he is guilty of eternal sin." Mark explains right after that Jesus said this because they were saying, "He has an unclean spirit." (Mark 3:30).
He asks a question, that's right. Jesus replies, "Who are My mother and My brothers?" (Mark 3:33). I think that question got the whole room's attention. Then He looks at the people around Him.
Jesus says the opposite, baker. Looking at those seated around Him, He says, "Here are My mother and My brothers!" (Mark 3:34). He calls them His family. That's a big word to give anybody.
False is right. Jesus looks at those seated in a circle around Him and says, "Here are My mother and My brothers!" (Mark 3:34). He calls them family, and that's a warm thing to hear.

Whoever does the will of God, you've got it. Jesus says, "For whoever does the will of God is My brother and sister and mother." (Mark 3:35). That's the door He opens to anybody. I'd have taken that welcome back when I was stuck in a junk drawer, friend.
